papers.title: Reference-Based Cell Type Deconvolution Using Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning in Spatial Transcriptomics with Ctdecon.
papers.summary: This paper introduces Ctdecon, a computational method for determining what cell types make up each spot in spatial transcriptomics data. It uses self-supervised contrastive learning, a deep learning approach that learns meaningful patterns from data without needing extensive manual labels, combined with a reference dataset of known cell types. The goal is to more accurately estimate cell type proportions in spatial transcriptomics experiments compared to existing deconvolution methods.
papers.why: Accurate cell type deconvolution is essential for correctly identifying and localizing interneurons within spatial transcriptomics data, which directly supports analysis of perineuronal net-associated neuronal populations in brain tissue.

papers.title: Imaging-based spatial isoform transcriptomics resolves transcript diversity at cellular and subcellular resolution
papers.summary: This paper presents an imaging-based spatial transcriptomics method capable of resolving different RNA isoforms, not just gene-level expression, while preserving their precise location within cells and subcellular compartments. This allows researchers to see where specific splice variants or transcript forms are positioned, such as near synapses, in dendrites, or within the nucleus. The approach expands spatial transcriptomics beyond gene counting into isoform-level resolution, adding a new layer of molecular detail to tissue imaging.
papers.why: Since neuronal subtypes like interneurons and perineuronal net-associated cells often rely on specific splice isoforms for local translation and compartment-specific function, this method could help the project map subcellular isoform distribution relevant to mitophagy and autophagy machinery in distinct neuronal compartments.

papers.title: MERFISHEYES: Web-based Visualization and Sharing Platform for Single-cell and Single-molecule Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: MERFISHEYES is a web-based tool designed to visualize and share single-cell and single-molecule spatial transcriptomics data, such as MERFISH outputs. It likely allows researchers to interactively explore gene expression patterns at both cellular and subcellular resolution directly in a browser. The platform aims to make sharing and collaborative analysis of complex spatial transcriptomic datasets more accessible without requiring specialized software.
papers.why: This tool could help visualize and share spatial transcriptomics data relevant to mapping mitophagy and autophagy markers across neuronal subtypes and perineuronal net-associated interneurons in the brain.

papers.title: Penconazole induces developmental neurotoxicity by activating autophagy and neuronal apoptosis in zebrafish.
papers.summary: This study examines how penconazole, a common agricultural fungicide, affects brain development in zebrafish embryos. The researchers found that exposure to this chemical triggers excessive autophagy (a cellular recycling process) and causes neurons to undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death). These combined effects lead to measurable neurodevelopmental toxicity in the exposed fish.
papers.why: While focused on a toxicology model rather than neurodegenerative disease or spatial omics, this paper offers relevant mechanistic insight into autophagy-driven neuronal death pathways that could inform interpretation of autophagy/mitophagy dysregulation in the brain more broadly.

papers.title: Msp1-dependent extraction promotes ubiquitylation of translocation-stalled mitochondrial precursor proteins
papers.summary: This paper studies Msp1, a protein that extracts mitochondrial precursor proteins stuck in the translocation machinery when they fail to properly enter mitochondria. The authors show that this extraction step actively promotes ubiquitylation of these stalled proteins, marking them for degradation. This reveals a quality control mechanism that clears defective mitochondrial protein import intermediates, helping maintain mitochondrial health.
papers.why: Although focused on yeast/cell biology mechanisms rather than neurons directly, this work on mitochondrial protein quality control and ubiquitylation is foundational to understanding mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal mitochondrial maintenance.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Transplantation Rejuvenates Aging Heart by Restoring Mitophagy Flux via the HIF-3α-BNIP3 Axis.
papers.summary: This study shows that transplanting healthy mitochondria into aging heart tissue can restore youthful function and structure. The researchers found that this treatment works by restoring mitophagy, the process by which cells clean up damaged mitochondria, through a specific molecular pathway involving HIF-3α and BNIP3. Restoring this mitophagy flux appeared to reverse signs of cardiac aging in the experimental model used.
papers.why: Although focused on heart tissue, this paper is relevant because it mechanistically links mitophagy flux restoration via HIF-3α-BNIP3 signaling to tissue rejuvenation, offering a molecular pathway framework that could inform studies of mitophagy dysregulation in aging neurons.

papers.title: SRC Promotes High Glucose-Induced Retinal Endothelial Dysfunction by Suppressing FUNDC1-Mediated Mitophagy in Diabetic Retinopathy.
papers.summary: This study investigates how high glucose levels in diabetes affect the cells lining retinal blood vessels. The researchers found that a protein called SRC becomes more active under high glucose conditions and blocks a mitochondrial quality control process called mitophagy, which normally relies on another protein called FUNDC1. By suppressing this mitophagy pathway, SRC contributes to dysfunction in retinal endothelial cells, a key feature of diabetic retinopathy.
papers.why: While focused on retinal rather than brain tissue, this paper's mechanistic insights into FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy regulation could offer transferable molecular principles for understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neurons.
